title: Content generation
thesis: Generating content pays only when players can perceive and care about the differences it makes: volume alone produces oatmeal, so the craft lies in the distribution (plain baselines with rare spikes), in correlation and theme, and in authoring data, corpora and fragments that a generator can combine meaningfully. Across names, text, histories, quests and puzzles, the talks converge on the same move: give the generator knowledge of what its pieces mean and make its output leave traces the player can act on, while remembering that players will read meaning into everything it produces, intended or not.

sections.heading: Why generate content, and how much is enough
sections.brief: Open with the case for generating content rather than writing it: Joseph Hewitt's framing of procgen as stage illusion, Everest Pipkin's list of what designers want from it (surprise, replayability, relief from hand-writing everything), Phillip Daigle's claim that even a Baldur's Gate decomposes into generatable parts, and Stella Mazeika's inventory of what randomizers vary. Then stage the central disagreement about volume: George Moromisato argues quantity is itself quality (NetHack's breadth), backed by Zack Johnson's point that variation gives repetitive play something to look forward to, Jon Perry's Mini and Max needing rewards everywhere, and Santiago Zapata's detective game that failed for lack of content; against them set Bruno Dias (procgen is not a force multiplier for cheap content), Cole Wehrle (too much content feels arbitrary, so Oath keeps a small deck), Rich Wilson's 'threat of infinite content', Max Kreminski's warning about extractive churn and Pipkin's tech-demo novelty that fades. Close with the usable standard Emtman and Austwick give (enjoyable once, different on the second pass) and briefly note the lineage in tabletop DM kits and Hack's borrowed AD&D monsters.

sections.heading: The oatmeal problem: making difference perceptible
sections.brief: Argue that mathematically distinct output is worthless if players cannot perceive the difference (Kate Compton's '10,000 bowls of oatmeal', as cited by Kreminski, Dias and Knipscher). The structural cause comes from Alex Byaly: generating attributes independently makes every region a sample of the same distribution, so nothing is worth visiting; his remedy is arbitrary local correlation, shown in Tales of Maj'Eyal's ego bundles and Dwarf Fortress's simulated history. Several talks converge on correlating or bundling at a higher level: Jason Grinblat varies the structure of Qud's societies, Emily Short's travel guide (via Darius Kazemi) gives each town one aesthetic element, and Liza Knipscher's Bioloom pushes scale and body shape to extremes and groups species into herds. Bruno Dias adds that text is a cheap source of perceptual difference, a lens that picks a new angle on identical underlying factors. End with practical guidance: correlate attributes, vary at the macro level, exaggerate the axes players can see, vary prefabs cosmetically (Sergio Garces), and make differences matter mechanically, as Isaac Karth says of Forgotten Beasts.

sections.heading: Baselines, spikes and rarity: shaping the distribution
sections.brief: Argue that memorable output depends on the shape of the distribution, not just its size. Lead with the convergence between Cat Manning's 'venom' principle (a few spiky characters against an unremarkable cast) and Elliot Trinidad's need for plenty of 'just some guy' names so the strange ones stand out. Then show the same idea as technique: rarity tiers in Emoji Aquarium and Mini and Max, Caves of Qud's percentage-gated book features, Bioloom's small chance of a wild body part, Kiss Garden's rare surreal moments, and Hintline 93's one-in-eight wrong numbers that keep the pool from feeling solved; Pacific Drive's fax machine draws from a deck so each story appears once. Then cover placement and pacing of items and creatures: Shattered Pixel Dungeon's interleaved shuffled decks for consistency versus Shiren's willingness to let great items appear early (set these against each other: consistency versus run-defining swings), the 'empty' spawn entry, Spelunky's wall-count treasure rule and its special-case spider, Six Day Stilt dropping depth constraints, and NetHack's artifact-wish odds. End with guidance on choosing a baseline, a rare tail, and whether to draw with or without replacement.

sections.heading: Constraint, theme and intention
sections.brief: Argue that a narrower, themed space usually beats a bigger one. Aaron A. Reed's case that limiting the generative space lets every output meet a higher authored standard (Subcutanean's hand-sculpted variation) pairs with Cole Wehrle's warning that obfuscation without intention becomes white noise. Show theme as the glue that lets recombined parts cohere: Matt Carney on Shadows of Doubt's noir elements and Qud's narrow sultan shrines inside a wide space, Bruno Dias's six alignments in Voyageur, Hades using mythology to generate parallel art and mechanics, Jim Shepard's field-guide tone for Dungeonmans monsters, Emoji Aquarium's scale-consistent emoji, and Ben Berman's point that small numbers feel designed. Set Wehrle's two observations against each other: random tables expose the whole space (and understanding undoes the illusion) while Tales of the Arabian Nights layers obscuring steps between choice and outcome. Close on mixing curated and generated material: the 'familiarity' rule (never generate a '57 Chevy), Love Island's degrees of curation, and Qud fans splitting their talk evenly between static and generated content.

sections.heading: Authoring content to combine: parts, tags, variants and possibility spaces
sections.brief: This is the practical core on how to author content a generator can multiply. Start from Atty Vohra: decide what output makes play interesting, then generate mechanics first and invent fiction to justify them, described as abstract adjective-verb pairs within a limited subspace; Jasper Cole and Leigh Alexander converge on building an explicit possibility space or category matrix (trigger/effect/target lists, borrowed schemes like Pokemon types) and mining its unused combinations for ideas. Then the data patterns: Spry Fox's variants, mods and tag references (Patrick Kemp) that make one config yield hundreds of items and flow into every system, Kate Compton's demand for painless authoring formats, Pierre Vigier's tag-and-trigger room details, and Thomas Robertson's dictionary/choreographer/director split with seeded attack records. Finish with modular assembly of functional and visual content and its pitfalls: Bioloom's sockets and the broken creatures from naive crossover, Test Tube Titans mutating a working template, Tea Garden's symmetry-constrained flowers, Sea of Rifts' kit pieces and stacking rules, and Ben Berman's warning that generated cards must look good as well as play good. Name the data structures concretely so a reader can implement them.

sections.heading: Names, languages and speech
sections.brief: Argue that names carry culture, and a generator should be designed for identity, not just variety. Lead with Sraëka-Lillian: generate a name generator per culture, aiming for output that is varied, internally cohesive and externally distinctive; Mark R Johnson's Ultima Ratio Regum converges on the same goal with per-culture syllable sets and world-specific naming archetypes. Then the phonology toolkit in implementable detail: a small, pronounceable sound inventory weighted by real-world prevalence, phonotactics to avoid 'consonant soup', recurring morphemes, and when to fix versus embrace a weird result. Contrast this with Blaseball's deliberately simple approach (Elliot Trinidad): random first plus last name, tuned by curating lists, themed name cycles, no saving cool names for bosses, and careful sourcing of real names. Cover place names (Dungeonmans' per-type schemes, Jim Shepard's warning that invented words must mean something) and speech: Johnson's case against learnable conlangs, culture-specific greetings and insults, and verbosity by culture and mood. Close with Kingdom of Loathing's named hobos and real baseball's surreal names as evidence that names alone make players care.

sections.heading: Assembled text: templates, grammars and fragments that know themselves
sections.brief: Open with why prose is harder than terrain (Bruno Dias: simplified language feels condescending) and the map of approaches: Dias's three (machine learning, plain text exposing a world model, assemblage) and Kazemi's linguistic versus simulationist split; this section takes assemblage, from Strachey's 1952 love letters to Tracery. Zack Johnson's principle that funny text lives between pure randomness and canned jokes, and Aaron A. Reed's that fragments tagged with sentiment, length and theme become tools for characterization (18 Cadence, Ice-Bound), are the two load-bearing ideas; Kate Compton's inline semantic tags in Hip Chef support Reed. Then the practical machinery: Kingdom of Loathing's combat messages from monster metadata, Duskers' log markup, Sea of Rifts' Tracery macros, Kiss Garden's minimal grammar, haiku syllable counting, and Caves of Qud's evolution from string concatenation to templates with chainable post-processors, which made localization (including Turkish agglutination) possible; note Compton's unsolved grammatical-gender problem. End with flavor text as an end in itself: NetHack hallucination names, robotfindskitten, Qud's 'whip up a meal' and Amber Spire's mixed voices.

sections.heading: Choosing the source: corpora, found text and curation
sections.brief: Argue, with Everest Pipkin, that generated text can only say what its source says, so choosing the corpus is the most important decision: big generic corpora average into blandness, while hand-curated niche sources give control of tone and ethics and let you credit authors; Kate Compton's note that shared word lists flatten tone converges. Show curation as craft: Caves of Qud's corpus half from its own text and half from tonally matched 19th-century books, Botnik splitting X-Files transcripts into per-character corpora and mashing unrelated corpora for comedy, Jamie Brew's Robot Karaoke scoring found lines by syllable count and phonetics from sources like Craigslist and tax forms, and Max Hawkins parsing verb phrases out of books. Then other mined sources: Tyler Coleman's adjective-noun item names matched by word vectors, real-world networks as card content (Ezra Szanton), scraped headlines in Neutrinowatch, search-API images in McMansion. Close with constrained forms (cut-ups, the Xenotext cipher) and the guidance that the corpus is a design artifact to be built deliberately.

sections.heading: Statistical text: Markov chains and language models
sections.brief: Argue that statistical text fits where its weakness becomes a feature. Jason Grinblat's Caves of Qud is the case study: Markov text is grammatical but semantically odd, which suits a library of ancient books whose context is lost; give the implementable details (sentence, paragraph and book lengths, title generation by shaving about 30 unwanted words, secrets embedded as unsplittable phrases after common hooks). Show how players read it: Ray sees the white-titled Markov books as signalling irrelevance, and Younès Rabii describes hand-written books with real clues hidden among them like crystals in smoke; Joe Sondow notes Markov bots make a different comedy from authored originals. Then set language models against templates: Robin Sloan argues LM output outlasts templates whose seams show and suggests using them as offline description engines, while Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster grant that generative AI is expressive and expansive but say it lacks consistency over time, which games need, and carries ethical risks of bias, unlicensed IP and hallucination. End with guidance on where each fits.

sections.heading: Generated history and culture: pasts that leave traces
sections.brief: Argue that generated history earns its cost only when it leaves traces the player can find and act on. Lead with Caves of Qud's villages, whose generated histories drive architecture, culture and quests, and Florence Smith Nicholls's 'object biographies'. Then walk through Qud's sultan system as the worked example: scope constrained to five sultans, history built event by event on a shared timeline, thematic domains as epithets, no imposed narrative arc because it is off the critical path, and outputs that become things in the world (legendary items with quests, cults, legendary monsters with faction grudges, journal secrets to trade, shrines whose murals disagree with the Tomb of the Eaters, the Mehmet fight in Joppa, signature dishes). Bring in other cultures and myths: Dwarf Fortress's planned myth generator with concrete in-world requirements, Mark Johnson's 'qualitative procedural generation', Spencer Egart's ritual generator (functional steps padded with flavour), Bad News's businesses founded by simulated people. Close with Mike Cook's exercise of comparing two games' history generators as one compares cities.

sections.heading: Generated systems: economies, tech trees and societies
sections.brief: Argue that a generated system can be content in itself when its structure varies between worlds. Mark Gritter's Emoji Economy gives the full algorithm: a goods-flow graph, utility maximisation with diminishing returns, regional copies with parts removed, and trade routes that restore utility (with its stated limits); Robin Mendoza adds that price movements can act as passive quest hooks. Dustin Freeman's tech-tree work is the other worked case: model a tree as nodes, weighted dependencies and topology, compare existing approaches (Sword of the Stars, Limit Theory, Alpha Centauri's blind research, Stellaris's card draws), and assign feasibility categories so universes feel distinct, with 'possible but undesired' the most interesting. Set Freeman's regret over Stellaris removing distinct FTL methods for balance as a flavour-versus-balance tension. Include Jonathan Lessard's fractal gift exchange that builds clans, tribes and kingdoms, and end with Freeman's open directions.

sections.heading: Quests: defining, generating and allocating them
sections.brief: Start from Kristen Yu's technical definition (a quest is a set of tasks earning rewards; each task specified by who, objective, monitoring, presentation and reward) and her Definition-Context-Purpose funnel, which replaces the main/side split and tells you to document a quest generator's context and purpose. Then the generation pipelines: Chronicles of Stampadia's database quests split into sub-events scattered across the dungeon (and the memory system out-of-order play forced), Caves of Qud's starting-village quests that point into the map, and Qud adding shrines because the quest design needed reasons to desecrate them. Jurie Horneman supplies the allocation engineering: picky versus non-picky requests, story-only location pools, a worst-case counting rule that proves the allocator safe, and the warning that tag-based selection can technically work yet keep serving the same quest. Close with player-parameterized quests (Robin Sloan's surveyed, mailed GPT-2 quests) and Yu's caveat that by her definition even Mario 1-1 is a quest.

sections.heading: Casting events: storylets, plots and oracles
sections.brief: Argue that much narrative content generation is selection and casting, not invention. Wildermyth's 'library of plays' (Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner) selects events whose roles the party can fill, weights specific events higher and scores heroes for each role; Max Kreminski's Star Freighter picks among eligible storylets and recycles every generated character into new roles; Paris Buttfield-Addison shows salience-based selection can implement bones files. Jasmine Otto's cyclic plot generation guarantees every setup pays off, even returning dead characters as ghosts, and Ian Holmes's graph grammar builds branching story graphs. Add the small cases (Dungeon Court's random pairings, Nathan Savant's motivation-keyed NPC dialogue). Then oracles from solo tabletop play (Cezar Capacle): probability-weighted yes/no answers and evocative word pairs the player interprets, curated toward a theme, complication oracles, and the trial and error of finding the right abstraction level. End with guidance contrasting authored-then-selected content with interpreted prompts.

sections.heading: Generated puzzles, riddles and traps
sections.brief: Lead with Josh Galecki's argument that a roguelike puzzle is trivial the second time, so puzzles must come from systems that generate new instances. Two worked systems converge on cross-referenced information: Mark Johnson's Ultima Ratio Regum riddles (complete pilgrimages unique per run, many scattered lead-ins converging on mutually referencing pieces, checkpoints whose clues are distributed into media, heavy cross-referencing and many alternative names for each referable thing) and Bjarke Alexander Larsen's Telegrams from the Quiet Train (corrupted databases derived from a hidden truth, each with its own field mapping and corruption texture, and varied starting information so each instance takes a new path). Add Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans's generic trap patterns that a generator reifies into any theme, given knowledge of room order and element interactions. Then smaller cases: Kingdom of Loathing's FAQ-generated zone and liar/truth-teller lock, McMansion's murder mystery, Andrew Plotkin on logic mazes and landmark mazes, Galecki's graph-theory sourcing, Chogue's accidental chess problems, and unknown-monster investigation ideas. End with design rules for keeping generated puzzles fair and deducible.

sections.heading: The meaning players make: attachment, apophenia and unintended readings
sections.brief: Close the chapter on the player's side: generated content gets its meaning from interpretation. Florence Smith Nicholls argues that incongruity and the uncanny texture of procgen spur interpretation; Younès Rabii's Tea Garden shows most flowers mean nothing but the rest evoke things players attach to. Converging evidence of attachment: Blaseball's text-only players inspired fan art (Trinidad, Joel Clark), Shawn Main felt random-table characters were more personal than chosen ones, and Seven Day Band lets the player author the content. The flip side is that meaning cannot be controlled: Tea Garden's fascist-looking flowers, Alexandra Leonhart's call to check a system's intent is readable to a diverse audience, Blaseball's diversity audit, retired names and living name lists, and Darius Kazemi's layered output filters and takedown policy. End with practical safeguards and Grinblat's suggestion that an evocative bug can become a premise.
